grammar_notes: mau at the end is known to mean 'place of'
cultural_notes: Woccon people have been documented under many historical names since 1521
Francisco Gordillo called them Guacaya in 1521
Early maps from 1606-1607 recorded variations like Wococon and Wokakon
John Lawson documented them as Woccoa in 1701
They were sometimes called 'Northward's Indians' and 'Parched Corn Indians' in the 1700s
Historical spellings include Wattomas, Wackamaws, Wacawns, Waccamaus, and Waccamawe
Colonial records from 1715 show multiple spelling variations in official documents
Maps from 1715-1795 recorded names like Waggoman, Wigomaw, Vocamas, and Wicomau
The variety of historical names reflects different colonial documentation sources over nearly 300 years
Woccon belonged to the Siouan linguistic stock, their closest relations being the Catawba
The meaning of the name Woccon is unknown
Also known as Waccamaw, Waccoommassus, and Cape Fear Indians
Woccon primarily lived between Neuse River and one of its affluents, near present-day Goldsboro, Wayne County, North Carolina
Waccamaw territory was from Winyah Bay up Waccamaw River to the Cape Fear, and somewhat to the Neuse River
Villages included Tooptatmeer and Yupwauremau, supposed to have been in Greene County
First mentioned by Lawson writing about 1701, who recorded 150 words of their language
Lawson's vocabulary showed Woccon was nearer Catawba than any other known variety of speech
Theory by Dr. Douglas L. Rights suggests they were originally the Waccamaw tribe in southeastern North Carolina and northeastern South Carolina
Took part against the whites in the Tuscarora Wars (1711-1715) and were probably extinguished as a tribe at that time
Remnants fled north with the Tuscarora, united with the Catawba, or combined with other Siouan remnants in the people later known as Croatan
Population estimated by Mooney (1928) at 600 in 1600
Lawson gives 120 warriors in 1701
Only southern group of eastern Siouan tribes other than the Catawba from which a vocabulary has been preserved
Documentation by John Swanton in the Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin of 1952
Woccon is the start of the word
Douglas L. Rights believed that the Woccon were the Waccamaw
1521 Francisco Gordillo possibly labels the Waccamaw as the Guacaya
Spanish entrance moved lots of tribes around, believed to have pushed Waccamaw Northwards
Almost no tribal nation is still in their exact same place due to Spanish entrada in 16th and 17th centuries
Many South Carolina tribes moved into the interior or up the coastline into North Carolina
Waccamaw bounced around between North and South Carolina often
Waccamaw still share significant ties with the Cheraw/Saraw, Waccamaw of NC, Lumbee, Cape Fear, and the Catawba
1606 Hondius-Mercator Map shows Woccon = Ocracoke Island
1662 William Hilton enters Cape Fear and arranges to purchase area from 100 or so natives
1663 Hilton bought land from Cape-Fear of Wattcoosa
1670 Name Waccamaw is used - English say they live along Waccamaw and PeeDee Rivers
Woccon were described as 'Caniballs, and Maneaters' by Richard Traunter in 1699
John Lawson recorded 150 words of Woccon language in 1701 and identified them as 'Siouan stock'
In 1701, Woccon had 120 fighting men, two towns named Yupwareremau and Tooptatmeer, and 500 total inhabitants
A group of Woccon broke away from the main settlement and relocated southward before 1701
Woccon participated in the Tuscarora War (1711-1713) as part of Captain Bull's Company in Barnwell's Army
Two Woccon were arrested in Virginia for leaving North Carolina without permission during the Tuscarora War period
The Woccon name disappears around the same time the Waccamaw name appears in historical records
Woccon were allied with South Carolina and referred to as 'Wachamau' in military correspondence
Settlers around Winyah Bay made war on Indians including Woccon to obtain slaves in the 1680s
Cape Fear Indians became 'Tribute Indians' after constant attacks and saved shipwreck victims
Waccamaw name is first mentioned in 1712 when James Moore Jr. asks them and Cape Fears to join him against the Tuscarora
Cape Fears were known to be with the Woccon often
In 1715, Waccamaw had 610 people living near Winyaw of Pee Dee River, with 200 Cape Fears living to the north
Waccamaw joined the Yamassee and Cheraw in the 1715 Yamassee War
On April 15, 1715, Waccamaw attacked South Carolina along with a large number of other native nations
Waccamaw were attacked by Maurice Moore in 1715, defeated, and many were taken captive and enslaved
Documentation comes from John Swanton in the Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin of 1952
Pre-1707 trading relationships existed with Thomas Smith who established a trading fort on Cape Fear
In 1716, head count was 4 towns and 610 people between the Waccamaw and Pee Dee Rivers
Charleston appointed William Watis Sr. as trading factor at Winyaw in 1716
Uauenee/Your Enee/Yahaunnah trading house was built in 1716 to be closer to the Pedee and Waccamaw
Waccamaw Chiefs visited Charleston in Fall 1717
William Waties named his plantation Witecaw/Wittecaw after probably an old village site in 1717
In 1718, the Waccamaw moved to the Black River according to trader Meredith Hughes
The Waccamaw made friendship with the Charraws in 1718, causing concern about potential war
The Waccamaw War occurred in 1718 with 60 killed or taken prisoner
In 1718, they were living between Black and Sampit Rivers at Winyah Bay with 100 fighting men
The famous Catawba Deerskin Map was presented in 1721 to Gov Francis Nicholson
Waccamaw town of several hundred people operated independently with own headman and fields
Waccamaw cooperated with Catawba nation
Some Waccamaw had confederated with the Catawba due to raids and enslavement by Seneca, Cherokee, and other groups
In 1723 some Waccamaw sought refuge with Winyaw and some with the Pedee
In 1723 Waccamaw petitioned to live on public land that used to belong to their ancestors
1725 Herbert Map shows Waccamaw largely in NC on Lumber River
In 1727 a Catawba leader reported that Waccamaws were living amongst them but maintained independence
The Waccamaw village was a half mile from that of the Catawba leaders in 1727
Mooney (1894) believes that the Waccamaw were finally incorporated with the Catawba
Alternative view suggests Waccamaw may have been absorbed by English settlements rather than joining Catawba
1727 Upper House Journal of SC reports Waccamaw live near Catawba
Waccamaw people were reported in Low Country in 1728/1733
In 1730 Waccamaw were blamed for shooting and killing Indian slave belonging to Meredith Hughes
Cape Fear and Waccamaw were still in parts of SC and NC in 1734
Lake Waccamaw had old Indian fields showing former habitation
Waccamaw were listed in Weaipee Town (Catawba area) in 1741 receiving commissions from English
War broke out between Waccommassus (Waccamaw) and SC in 1749
Waccamaw were described as 'one of the small friendly tribes' in 1751
Last reference to the name 'Waccamaw' was in 1755 when they were called 'Settlement Indians'
Many Waccamaw fled to NC swamps in 1778 when SC Council provided them protection
Dimery was in Drowning Creek Community (modern Robeson County NC) from 1780-1795
Dimery moved to live with 'Indians of Marlboro' in 1795
John Dimery purchased 300 acres at 'Dog Bluff' in 1810
Three 'Indian families' lived in Dog Bluff according to 1850 Census: Sarah Cook, Cockren Thompkins, and John Demery
Dog Bluff residents were listed as 'Colored Voters' in 1876 Horry News article
Dimery Church was formed in 1878, later becoming Bethel Missionary Baptist
Church was constructed in 1886 called 'Dimery Church'
Holly Hill Free Will Baptist Church was established in early 1900s
Woccon was most closely related to Catawba within the Siouan linguistic family
Woccon is part of the Eastern Siouan branch, which includes Catawba and Woccon
The Siouan linguistic family has two branches: Eastern Siouan includes Catawba and Woccon
Pine Level School was founded in 1908, also called Dimery School
In 1922 Pine Level was reclassified from 'Negro School' to Indian/'Special' School
Pine Level School closed in 1955 due to low enrollment
The modern tribe was formed in 1992 with initial organizational meeting on Oct. 17th
The tribe received recognition in 2005
HR1942 was signed in 2021
Historical miscegenation cases involved tribal members from 1905-1921
Daniel Alford was remembered as being an 'Indian Doctor'
The Dimery Settlement was noted for having 'Indian Blood' in 1921 newspaper articles
Woccon is a dormant Eastern Siouan language
The Woccon language closely resembled Catawba, and was considered one of two Catawban languages, which are part of the Siouan language family
Waccon was a subdivision of the Waccamaw
Western Siouan languages include Dakota, Ofo, Tutelo, Biloxi
John Lawson documented a vocabulary of Woccon in 1709 in 'A New Voyage to Carolina'
Academic research on Woccon includes work by R. Carter (1980) on genetic affiliations and historical significance
Blair A. Rudes (1985) studied Woccon number words
Contemporary language revitalization efforts are documented by Passmore, Sayers, Bradley, and Lomboy (2024)
Woccon is a coastal Catawban language
Woccon phonology and morphology have been reconstituted by linguist B.A. Rudes
Woccon is part of the Siouan language family
Historical documentation of Woccon comes from colonial records including the Tuscarora Expedition letters
John Lawson's 1709 voyage to Carolina provides early documentation of Woccon people
Colonial records from South Carolina and North Carolina contain references to Woccon people
Woccon people were documented in journals of Indian trade commissioners from 1710-1718
Richard Traunter's travels in 1698 and 1699 provide early contact period documentation
Woccon is documented in historical records from the British Public Record Office relating to South Carolina from 1663-1770
Early Carolina narratives from 1650-1708 contain references to Woccon people
Frank G. Speck documented Siouan tribes of the Carolinas including connections to Catawba and Tutelo sources in 1935
Woccon is classified as a Siouan tribe of the Carolinas based on anthropological and documentary sources
